inline.s: Practical Training Materials
Living in Awareness
Its practice has steps by which to enter;
its realization has a truth that is won for oneself.
Perseverance is passion for long-term goals, together with persistence.
Excellence in work comes from diligence, and is ruined by play;
Carve without letting up, and even metal and stone can be engraved.
The three “froms” and the one “great”:
strictly, under hard conditions, and starting from real combat;
great volume of training.
Diligently cultivate discipline, concentration, and wisdom; extinguish greed, anger, and delusion.
[Under hard conditions] Practice only in the “learning zone.” For details see
Ten Thousand Hours of Deliberate Practice Make a Genius
Deliberate practice:

Expert-level performance is trained up gradually, and the key to effective progress lies in finding a series of small tasks and having the trainee complete them in order, so that the goal can be reached. These small tasks must be ones the trainee just cannot yet do, and yet can just manage to learn and master. Completing this kind of practice requires the trainee to concentrate intensely, which makes it entirely different from routine or entertaining practice.

Whether we are learning small life skills such as playing ball, driving, playing an instrument, or cooking, or improving key work abilities such as writing, sales, programming, or design, none of it is possible without a great deal of practice. But we usually have a great misunderstanding about practice: isn’t practice just repetition over and over? No! Mere repetition is only ‘
naive practice
’, and it brings no progress. ‘
Correct practice
’ requires good guidance (teaching yourself is simply being your own guide), goals, and feedback.

inline.s: The goal of awareness in Buddha-recitation is: faith and vows, holding the name, one mind undisturbed, and ensuring rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss beyond doubt. This is something every reciter of the Buddha’s name can attain through diligent effort.

Awareness in Buddha-recitation is based on a focused, continuous, and enduring power of awareness, in order to attain one mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation. It is therefore divided into two great parts: preliminary practice and Buddha-recitation — the Preliminary Practices section and the Buddha-Recitation section. In the preliminary practices, one cultivates the power of awareness through training in “awareness of movements,” “awareness of sensations,” “awareness of breathing,” “awareness of the present moment,” and “awareness of thoughts.” Once a solid foundation has been laid, one can then devote all one’s strength to Buddha-recitation, so as to attain one mind undisturbed in holding the name.

For a Chan practitioner, the Preliminary Practices section is also the foundation for contemplating the mind and practicing Chan. With this solid foundation, contemplating the mind and practicing Chan come naturally and smoothly.

inline.s: Living in awareness.

There are two kinds of thoughts. One is the autonomous thought: a thought we ourselves actively give rise to, one we are master of, which begins when we want it to begin and stops when we want it to stop. This is called an intention — for example, the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name. The other is the non-autonomous thought, over which we have no mastery, whose arising and ceasing are not up to us. This kind of thought is called a drifting thought — for example, “the ceaseless chatter of self-talk in the head,” commonly known as delusive thinking.

Whether one recites the Buddha’s name, recites mantras, contemplates the mind, practices Chan, chants sutras, or bows to the Buddha, if one is to gain power, one must extinguish drifting thoughts. Great Master Yongming said:
“Focus the mind on one point, and there is nothing that cannot be done.”
(Record of the Mirror of the School)

People either wallow in the past or calculate the future; they are forever spinning delusive thoughts. This is a habit rooted deep since beginningless kalpas, like a drug addiction, and it is the source of suffering. In today’s society, with its material abundance, people no longer endure the real sufferings of hunger and cold; their main suffering often comes instead from mental torment. Its culprit is the drifting thought — the uncontrollable, endless drifting thought of pondering and rehashing. For example, a matter is long past, and you clearly know it will have no effect on the present or the future, and yet “scarce has it left the brow, and it is back in the heart”: irrepressible painful memories gnaw at your mind, and give rise to many physical illnesses.

The harm of drifting thoughts goes far beyond mental torment and being the cause of illness. What is more serious and more terrible is that they are the hallucinogen that clouds the spirit-consciousness and casts it into the cycle of rebirth. Everyone knows the saying
“When the mad mind does not rest, that resting itself is bodhi.”
So then, since we already understand this principle, why will the mad mind still not rest? It is the drifting thought making mischief.

To be free of birth and death and escape the cycle of rebirth, one must stop taking this hallucinogen — one must extinguish drifting thoughts. When drifting thoughts are extinguished, one naturally awakens; the right wisdom of prajñā appears before one, and at the moment of death one can be clear and mindful, ensuring rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. But if in ordinary times one is all day long amid a flurry of delusive thoughts, unable to be one’s own master, then at the moment of death, beset and seared by countless sufferings, how can one keep the spirit clear and not lose right mindfulness? Therefore, to ensure rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death, the skill of extinguishing drifting thoughts in ordinary times is of the utmost importance. Great Master Yinguang said:
“If you wish not to be confused at the moment of death, you must have genuine practice in ordinary times. If in ordinary times you drift along casually, how can you be clear at the moment of death?”
(Supplement Three to the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang,
Letter in Reply to the Layman Lü Zhiming)

How can one extinguish drifting thoughts and break free from delusive thinking? The wondrous method is: awareness! Awareness is the sharp weapon that extinguishes drifting thoughts. When there is awareness, there is no drifting thought; if a drifting thought arises, that shows awareness has been lost at that moment, and it should be taken up again at once. When awareness becomes continuous, one naturally dwells in the state of being aware yet without thought or thinking. The Sutra of the Buddha-Treasury says:
“The Buddhas’ anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is entirely without thinking and without thought.”

Since awareness and drifting thoughts cannot coexist — where there is awareness there is no drifting thought, and where there is a drifting thought awareness has been lost — why is it that sometimes awareness and drifting thoughts seem to be present at the same time? It is because awareness is not focused and continuous, and has not yet been linked into stretches; thus there appear alternating moments of awareness and moments of drifting thought, and one mistakenly supposes the two to be coexisting. So in working at awareness, the first task is to link awareness into stretches. Once awareness forms stretches, within those stretches there is naturally no drifting thought. In ordinary times, one should as far as possible accomplish this: to be aware without drifting thoughts, and to be freed from the control of drifting thoughts.

The core of the preliminary stage is this: by cultivating a focused, continuous, and enduring power of awareness, one avoids falling into the world of the head as much as possible; and the moment one does fall in, one must become aware of it at once and break free of it. In one’s practice one must hold to this point at all times and in all places; the depth of one’s practice is measured by this as well.
Question: Since drifting thoughts and awareness cannot coexist, then what is the saying “the moment a thought arises, one is aware” about?

Answer: The state of “the moment a thought arises, one is aware” comes when the power of awareness is already very strong, so that one is aware at all times. Although now and then there is a slip and a drifting thought arises (at which moment awareness is lost), awareness is quickly restored and one becomes aware of the drifting thought that just occurred. If the power of awareness is not strong, one often has to indulge in delusive thinking for a while, or even for a spell, before one can become aware of it. So “the moment a thought arises, one is aware” is the result of a strong power of awareness. In study and practice, this saying is also often used to train the power of awareness — the moment a delusive thought arises, one must see it. At the same time, the strength of one’s awareness can also be judged by how long delusive thinking lasts. Great Master Guifeng said:
“The moment a thought arises, one is aware; once aware of it, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone.”
(Preface to the Collection of Chan Sources and the Various Expositions)
Question: Why do drifting thoughts arise?

Answer: When the manas-consciousness (the mind-root) spontaneously grasps at mental objects within the ālaya-consciousness and transmits them to the sixth consciousness (the mind-consciousness), the thought that arises is a drifting thought. (
For a discussion of the manas-consciousness, the ālaya-consciousness, and the mind-consciousness, see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
in this academy’s study garden,
the section “How the Consciousness-Mind Operates”

) The manas-consciousness cannot do two things at once. When it is aware, it cannot grasp at mental objects; when it grasps at mental objects, awareness is certainly lost. This is the principle that “where there is awareness, there is no drifting thought.” It is like a person who, when acting as a police officer enforcing the law, will not steal; if he goes off to steal, then he is not enforcing the law. The Chan school’s inquiry into the critical phrase blocks the mind-root
(keeping the mind-root from grasping at mental objects)
and so stops the flow of delusive thinking. Great Master Hanshan said:
“Great Master Dahui, for instance, taught only the inquiry into the critical phrase, striking a venomous blow; his sole aim was to make you put your thieving mind
(the emotional consciousness)

to death. ... This above is the tongs and hammer the old man Dahui habitually used; his meaning was simply to have you block the mind-root with the critical phrase so that the flow of delusive thinking cannot proceed, and right there where it cannot proceed, to see your original face.”
(Dream Roaming Collection,
Essential Pointers for Chan Practice)
[Flow of delusive thinking] The arising and ceasing, the shifting flow, of delusive thinking. [When the flow of delusive thinking cannot proceed] The flow of delusive thinking comes to rest.
Question: What are delusive thoughts about?
Answer: There are two kinds of thinking: autonomous and non-autonomous. What is generally called delusive thinking is non-autonomous thinking, drifting thoughts in unbroken succession.

The process by which the consciousness-mind takes account of and ponders sense objects is: feeling → perception → volition → consciousness. “Feeling” is the taking in that occurs when the six sense faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind) contact the six sense objects (forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, mental objects). “Perception” is the thinking (analyzing, judging, synthesizing) that arises depending on “feeling”; the basis for its analysis and judgment is the mental objects that the seventh consciousness (manas) draws out of the eighth consciousness (ālaya). “Volition” is the mental activity (inner formation, such as liking and disliking, favoring and rejecting) that arises depending on “thinking,” along with the issuing of action commands to body and speech, and so on — this is the creation of karma. “Consciousness” is the gathering together of all the information from the preceding three links — feeling, perception, and volition — into a synthesized distinguishing aspect, the karma-consciousness, which is then fed through the seventh consciousness into the eighth consciousness to be stored away for later use. These are what are called karmic seeds, also called mental objects, and they are what the manas-consciousness grasps at.

[Karmic seeds] The karma created by sentient beings is stored in the ālaya-consciousness; because it can produce manifest activity and so flower and bear fruit, it is called a seed. Karmic seeds are also called karmic habitual tendencies, or simply seeds or habitual tendencies. They exert a latent influence, even a controlling influence, on people’s thinking and behavior.

When one is engaged in delusive thinking, the mind-root (manas) grasps at mental objects (karmic seeds) within the ālaya-consciousness and gives rise to “feeling”; thereupon this cycle of the consciousness-mind — “feeling → perception → volition → consciousness” — begins. Without people’s being aware of it, the manas-consciousness keeps transmitting onward, and so drifting thoughts follow one after another: this is delusive thinking. For ordinary people, delusive thinking is extremely common; they may even be working while indulging in delusive thinking. When delusive thinking becomes severe, mad mind appears. That is to say, you cannot stop the delusive thinking even if you want to, and this is extremely painful.
Question: Then how does one stop delusive thinking?

Answer: Delusive thinking is able to continue because the mind-root (manas) keeps grasping at mental objects (karmic seeds) within the ālaya-consciousness and transmitting them to the mind-consciousness (the sixth consciousness) to be thought about. So as long as the mind-root (manas) no longer grasps at mental objects within the ālaya-consciousness, then because no fuel is supplied, the fire of delusive thinking dies out. Besides grasping at mental objects, the manas-consciousness has another function: awareness. And the manas-consciousness can perform only one function at a time. When it is aware, it cannot grasp at mental objects; if it is grasping at mental objects, awareness is lost. This is the “drifting thoughts and awareness cannot coexist” spoken of above. Therefore the method for stopping delusive thinking, as described above, is: awareness. You can verify this principle yourself: at the very moment you are aware in a focused and continuous way, there is no delusive thinking. The essential point of practice is to make awareness focused, continuous, and enduring. As the saying goes: If the seventh consciousness does not die, how can the dharma-body live? (If the manas-consciousness still keeps grasping at mental objects without cease, how can one realize the dharma-body?) The Treatise on the Universal Ground of All Things says:
“Because of
(owing to)

failure to comprehend the one dharma-realm, the mind is not in accord, and a thought suddenly arises, which is named ignorance. This ignorance is also called the seventh consciousness, also called manas; it specializes in calculating and clinging to a self, and is the master of discrimination and the root of ignorance. It travels to and fro between the sixth and eighth
(between the sixth and eighth consciousnesses)
, transmitting onward and outward, obstructing the great luminous brightness and veiling the original.”
[Traveling to and fro between the sixth and eighth] For details see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
. [One dharma-realm] The single dharma-realm, that is, the true aspect of all dharmas. On the true aspect of all dharmas (for details see
The True Aspect of All Dharmas

Awareness in Buddha-recitation is based on a focused, continuous, and enduring power of awareness, in order to attain one mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation. Therefore, in the preliminary practices, one cultivates the power of awareness through training in “awareness of movements,” “awareness of sensations,” “awareness of breathing,” “awareness of the present moment,” and “awareness of thoughts.” Once a solid foundation has been laid, one can then devote all one’s strength to the practice of awareness in Buddha-recitation, so as to attain one mind undisturbed in holding the name.

A focused, continuous, and enduring power of awareness is the foundation of awareness in Buddha-recitation. With this solid foundation and diligent Buddha-recitation, one is certain to attain one mind undisturbed. Therefore the foundation must first of all be made firm!

To make the foundation firm, one must expend great effort and undergo bitter training. Practicing the basics may sometimes feel monotonous and dry, but in fact this is precisely the best time for forging the mind and cultivating concentration; and once the skill runs deep, bitterness ends and sweetness comes, and there is a delight all its own. On this point, Mr. Li Fengshan wrote in his Secret Manual of Training:

Whatever one does, one must always begin from the basics. Training skills even more so: one must begin by training the basic exercises. Horse stance and stake stance were exercises I can never forget, painful yet greatly beneficial. At that time the master required us to practice the “one-character stake” well (see the figure below). For Chinese martial arts must put effort into the stake stance. In ordinary boxing practice the emphasis is on continuity and speed is relatively fast; but in practicing the stake stance, one must set angles, adjust posture, and train endurance and power. To be able to hold the stake stance for a considerable time does not depend on physical strength but on stability of mind. At the age of ten-something, to speak of stability of mind was truly a little difficult. But every time the master watched us train, he would say, “Sink a little lower, sink a little lower,” strictly adjusting our movements. Sometimes, after squatting a long while and growing tired, a stifled anger would arise, even turning into wrath; once hatred arose in the mind, one could squat no longer. Only later did I discover that if I still had wrath in my mind, my mind became narrow, and there was no way to keep training. I told myself: I must trust the master; if the master makes this demand, there must be a reason; however the master says to do it, that is how I will do it. Once my attitude shifted, strange to say, my mind became steady. Naturally I could squat lower and longer. I also discovered that in the past, when I did horse stance, my body was too tense at the start, so my breathing came in great gasps and pants, and sometimes I even held my breath; now that the mind was settled, not only could I squat longer, my breathing was smooth. From this I also realized how great the function of the mind is. The mind can lift you up, and it can drag you down; it can save people, and it can harm people. Those who constantly excuse themselves, who are too narrow, or who hold no expectations for themselves, can never squat long. Only by making the mind one-pointed, thinking of nothing else, and bringing the mind into a state of non-doing, can one be calm in spirit and untroubled in breath.
The plum blossom’s fragrance comes from the bitter cold

There are many objects of awareness — movements, sensations, breathing, scenery, the body, thoughts, and so on. All of them can be used to cultivate the power of awareness and cut off delusive thinking. But among them, awareness of movements is the easiest — one need only not forget it — so the preliminary practices begin with awareness of movements as the way to cultivate the power of awareness.

Awareness of movements means clearly perceiving the progress of a movement and the sensations the movement gives rise to. For example, when walking, be aware of the working of the feet and of the sensation when the soles meet the ground; when washing the face, be aware of the movements of the hands, the temperature of the water, the sensation when the towel touches the face, and so on. Of course, one may also be aware only of the progress of the movement. The essential point of awareness is: focus the mind on one point, and delusive thoughts do not arise. So do whatever you find best enables you to meet this requirement. While aware, you may silently say “aware” in the mind to help yourself gather your attention on awareness.

When aware of movements, one should be focused: whatever one does, do it single-mindedly, without delusive thinking. For example, when dressing or eating, if one is aware of the movements and free of delusive thinking, that is the state of awakening; if one does the same things while indulging in delusive thinking, that is the state of delusion (ignorance) — the same task is done, but “the mind is used differently,” and the consequences are as far apart as heaven and earth. As long as one does not lose awareness, carrying firewood and hauling water are all practice.
Returning to the Present Moment

: its author writes in this book, “When I was in India, I stayed on the second floor of a meeting house. In the course of a day I had to go up and down the stairs many times, and each time I would investigate the structure of each step of the climb, the working of the knees, and how the weight shifted. This is a fascinating process; we must hold this kind of interest toward all our activities. To see clearly, to investigate how everything happens.”
It should be specially explained:
1. When aware, one must not only be aware of the object of awareness (the perceived), but also know that one is being aware (the perceiver) — do not sink into the object of awareness.
2. So-called “focus” does not mean staring fixedly at the object of awareness, but rather not letting the attention wander (lose attentiveness) so that delusive thoughts arise.
3. Putting the above two together: when aware, be a relaxed, at-ease, and calm observer, observing your own movements.

Beginners should start by training the supporting exercises. This has two advantages. First, through training the supporting exercises one comes to understand the essential point of awareness of movements, and then applies it to every movement of daily life. Second, practitioners often ask: what should I do when delusive thoughts come thick and fast? Now, with the precious sword of the supporting exercises in hand, if delusive thoughts come thick and fast, one immediately does the supporting exercise, and the delusive thoughts cease of themselves. In this way, the delusive thoughts that plague us become sparring partners for our practice.

This supporting exercise borrows Mr. Li Fengshan’s “flat swing exercise.” It is a very good exercise: it harmonizes the five viscera and six bowels, invigorates the blood and qi, replenishes oxygen and expels toxins, and makes the joints of the whole body supple.
The key points of the exercise are: no drifting thoughts, and perceiving each movement with perfect clarity, so as to cultivate a focused, continuous, and enduring power of awareness.

The method is this: feet apart to shoulder width, both hands raised level with palms facing down at shoulder height, fingers extended, a smile on the face. To begin, swing both hands backward, then return to the horizontal, swinging forward and back in this relaxed, natural way. The count is: one, two, three, four, five, six. For the first four counts, the count is called as the hands swing backward. “Five, six” are the squat and straightening of the knees (two bounces): on the fifth swing, the hands go back and one bends the knees slightly into a small squat, calling “five”; then the hands come forward, both knees straighten, and one calls “six.” The movements should be gentle and relaxed, forming a natural resonance; there is no need to squat very low. To finish, the hands slowly come to a stop and return naturally to the sides of the body; the eyes close gently, the breath is made even, the whole body relaxes, and then the eyes slowly open. (There are videos of the flat swing exercise online, which you may watch, for example:
Standard Demonstration of the Flat Swing Exercise (video)
) After practicing, slowly drink a cup of warm boiled water; this further helps the circulation of blood and qi and steadies the movement of qi.

The flat swing exercise is a movement that easily reaches the extremities. The ten fingers are connected to the heart, and so it can produce a thorough return flow, purify the five viscera and six bowels, and let the hundred illnesses adjust themselves. Once a day for thirty minutes, it brings enormous benefit to body and mind. The first ten minutes achieve circulation through the whole body; the second ten minutes begin to reach the places in the body that are overtaxed; the third ten minutes begin to adjust the sites of illness, attaining the realm where softness overcomes hardness.

What must be especially stressed here is: do the flat swing exercise at least once a day, thirty minutes each time. The reason for laying down such a hard-and-fast rule is that, besides being a cultivation of concentration in movement and being very effective for cultivating the power of awareness, this hand movement has another very important function: it cultivates in oneself good psychological qualities and a good psychological state. Doing these movements is not at all difficult; anyone can do them, and anyone can keep them up. And yet the fact is otherwise. Where does the problem lie? It lies in our habitual nature: the mind will not quiet down, will not settle — like a wild horse, like a sly monkey, like a mad elephant. You can try an experiment: while practicing, if the mind becomes fretful, or if you think of other things you have to do, you immediately cannot go on. But if you turn the thought around — practice is like saving your head from fire, it is the foremost matter; can what you want to do really not wait even thirty minutes? If I cannot even see this exercise through, what practice am I doing? — the mind immediately becomes cool and steady, and you can finish the practice well. So the secret of “when the mind turns, the circumstances turn” lies exactly here. If there really is something very important that must be done at once or thought through at once, then stop, finish it and think it through, and then practice with no lingering concerns.

Of course, those with a stronger healing reaction may reduce the practice time, and once the body is back to normal, gradually return to thirty minutes each time. If the body is not suited to standing and squatting, swinging while seated will do as well and is equally effective.
The Sutra of the Essential Secret Methods of Chan says:
“With one mind, practice diligently, as if saving your head from burning
(burning)
, and let the mind not be self-indulgent.”

For practice, good psychological qualities and a good psychological state are very important; hence the venerable masters of old undertook all kinds of austerities to temper themselves, so as to cultivate good psychological qualities and a good psychological state.

There is another practice for cultivating good psychological qualities and a good psychological state: eat one meal of awareness each day (perceiving every movement of eating with perfect clarity, without letting the mind wander east and west). Admonish yourself: if I cannot even see this practice through, what practice am I doing! After doing it for a long time, when the mind has become cool and steady, you will feel the wonder of it.
Mencius said:

“Thus, when Heaven is about to lay a great burden on a man, it must first distress his mind and will, fatigue his muscles and bones, starve his body and skin, leave him utterly destitute, and disrupt whatever he does, so as to stir his mind, toughen his nature, and increase
(augment)
what he was not capable of.”

Translation: Therefore, when Heaven is about to send a great mission down upon such a person, it must first make his mind and will perilous and bitter, tire his muscles and bones, bring hunger and cold upon his body, reduce him to utter poverty and peril, disrupt everything he does, and bring him repeated setbacks. By these means his spirit is tempered and refined and raised up, his character made resolute and courageous and unyielding through a hundred trials, and his capacities increased beyond what he originally had. (For full annotations see
Born in Sorrow and Perishing in Ease

In insight meditation, awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen is often used as the basic exercise for training the power of awareness, with excellent results. On this, the Venerable Mahasi of Burma gave a penetrating teaching:

“With each breath the abdomen rises and falls. You should begin to note this movement, observing the abdomen with attention. When you breathe in you will find the abdomen rising; when you breathe out the abdomen falls. As the abdomen rises, note ‘rising’ inwardly; as it falls, note ‘falling’ inwardly. If the movement is not clear, you may place your hand on the abdomen. But do not change the breathing; do not deliberately slow it down or speed it up, and do not breathe too forcefully. If you change the breathing, it will make you feel tired. Breathe naturally, and note the rising and falling movement of the abdomen. Note with the mind (or label), not by reciting aloud.

(Note: there are mainly two common ways of breathing: chest breathing and abdominal breathing. Chest breathing relies chiefly on the movement of the ribs and breastbone; on inhalation the chest expands front to back and side to side. Because the air goes directly into the lungs when breathing this way, the chest cavity expands and the abdomen stays flat. The breathing here is abdominal breathing in its natural mode, that is, on inhalation the abdominal muscles gently expand (the abdomen rises), and on exhalation the abdominal muscles gently contract (the abdomen falls). Compared with chest breathing, this way of breathing has many more benefits for bodily health.)

In insight meditation, names and what is said are not important; what truly matters is to know, to be aware. Note the rising of the abdomen from the very beginning of the movement until the whole rising process is complete, as though seeing it with the eyes. The same with noting the falling movement. When noting the rising movement, make the aware mind one with the rising movement; movement and awareness must be in step, like dropping a stone that strikes the target dead center. The same with the falling movement.

When noting the movement of the abdomen, the mind may wander here and there. Then note inwardly, ‘wandering, wandering.’ After noting in this way once or twice, the wandering mind will stop, and at that point we return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen. If you find the mind has arrived somewhere, label ‘arriving, arriving,’ and then return to the movement of the abdomen. If you think of meeting someone, label ‘meeting, meeting,’ and then return to the rising and falling of the abdomen. If you think of someone and talk with him, label ‘talking, talking.’

In short, whenever any thought or recollection arises, it must be noted (or labeled). If you imagine, label ‘imagining.’ If you think, label ‘thinking.’ If you plan, label ‘planning.’ If you perceive, label ‘perceiving.’ If you recollect, label ‘recollecting.’ If you feel happy, label ‘happy.’ If you feel bored, label ‘bored.’ If you feel glad, label ‘glad.’ If you feel discouraged, label ‘discouraged.’ Noting all these activities of the mind is called the ‘contemplation of mind.’
When it is noted, it disappears. Then we return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen.” (For details see
Practical Insight Meditation
[Turning without stop] A figure for working day and night without rest.

For a practitioner, what one does is not important; what matters is the state one is in while doing it. If one is in a state of awareness, even a tiny matter has great significance; if one has lost awareness, then no matter how great the matter one does, it is no more than planting the cause of rebirth.

In daily life, whatever you do, be aware of every movement: be aware when dressing and eating, be aware when walking and opening a door, be aware when making a phone call, be aware when moving the mouse in front of the computer,

To cultivate the power of awareness quickly, one must keep awareness of movements unbroken throughout the twenty-six hours of the day — that is, day and night — and never warm up for one day and freeze for ten. When there is movement, one must be aware; when there is no movement, one does the supporting exercises or small movements of one’s own devising in order to be aware. In fact, some of the routine matters of daily life — dressing, eating, washing the face, brushing the teeth, getting up, sitting down, opening a door, walking, and so on — can all be gathered into an exercise of awareness of movements, done with keen interest, so as to form the habit of never being apart from awareness. As the saying goes, “The fist never leaves the hand, the song never leaves the mouth.” Our practice must have this same spirit: in every movement, never apart from awareness. The moment you open your eyes in the morning, remind yourself: today I must keep aware, aware in everything. For example, when drinking water or eating, was every mouthful perceived? When sitting down or standing up, was it all perceived? When walking, was every step perceived? Do these few things well first, and then unfold it all. One must cultivate the habit of awareness of movements; this point is of the utmost importance. In fact, practice is simply cultivating the mind and rectifying conduct, and its key is to overcome karmic obstacles and transform bad habits — for example, transforming the habit of endlessly indulging in delusive thinking into the habit of endlessly being aware.

Deeply believe that “one share of cultivation, one share of harvest.” So in practice, ask only about the cultivation and not about the harvest; once the power of awareness has been cultivated, all problems are solved as they arise. Reflect constantly: Am I aware? Master, keep wide awake!
[Wide awake] Clear in mind and spirit. For a practitioner, sinking into delusive thinking or into drowsiness is both a lack of clarity, because one is not one’s own master.

To have awareness turning without stop (never pausing): throughout the twenty-six hours of the day, be aware of every movement, diligent and unremitting. It is said that a fly once came and settled on the Buddha’s face, and the Buddha lightly brushed it away with his hand. Then he made the gesture of brushing again. The disciples asked in surprise: “World-Honored One, the first time you brushed with your hand was to drive away the fly; what was the second brush for?” The Buddha answered: “The first was an unconscious movement, made without awareness, so I made the movement a second time with awareness, to correct it.” This manifestation by the Buddha was to teach his disciples:
Every movement must be perceived with perfect clarity; a movement made without awareness is ignorance, and one must correct it at once.

In fact, the many devices of the Chan school also only want you to block the mind-root so that the flow of delusive thinking cannot proceed, and right there where it cannot proceed, to see your original face. To block it by awareness of movements is truly far less effort, and no matter whether one’s faculties are sharp or dull, everyone can do it. You must understand that to be aware of movements while free of thinking and thought is to cultivate concentration in movement; never slight it as shallow and easy.
In the Great Discourse on the Establishing of Mindfulness, the Buddha says:

“When a monk is walking, he clearly knows, ‘I am walking.’ When standing, he clearly knows, ‘I am standing.’ When sitting, he clearly knows, ‘I am sitting.’ When lying down, he clearly knows, ‘I am lying down.’ In whatever posture, he clearly knows it. Thus he contemplates the body internally, he contemplates the body externally, and he contemplates the body both internally and externally. He contemplates the phenomena continually arising in the body, he contemplates the phenomena continually ceasing in the body, and he contemplates the phenomena continually arising and ceasing in the body. Thus he clearly knows, ‘This is the body!’ He has accomplished the state of mere awareness and mere observation, transcending clinging, no longer coveting anything in the world of body and mind. Monks! This is how a monk contemplates the body as body.”
So how does one cultivate awareness and keep it at all times and in all places? How does one turn daily life into practice and delight in it? The Collected Works of Master Thich Nhat Hanh says:

You may ask: while washing dishes, binding books (binding books was Master Thich Nhat Hanh’s daily work, and in his book he tells how he turned this work into practice), or working in a factory or office, how exactly does one cultivate awareness? I think you must find the answer yourself. As long as you do your best to keep the inner light of awareness bright, you will in the end discover the way that suits you.”

For a Chan master, when washing dishes, the sacred and the mundane can coexist and interpenetrate without conflict. To be aware, while washing dishes, of the process of the hands touching the dishes and the water is an experience full of the sacred and the wondrous; but the key point still lies in washing continuously and with focus on the present moment.”

There are many other things to do in life: tending the garden, cooking and washing clothes, cleaning bowls and chopsticks, binding books, writing. Perhaps these are not as interesting as drinking tea or walking on the hillside, but if you do them with full awareness, you will find them quite delightful as well. Even washing the bowls after a full meal is a pleasurable joy; every bowl we wash is a miracle.”

Every thought and every movement within awareness is sacred. In this luminous field, the boundary between the sacred and the mundane has dissolved. I admit that I take a long time to wash the dishes, but I live in the present moment at every moment, and my mind is very happy. Washing dishes is both means and end — in other words, washing dishes is not only to clean the plates but also for the sake of washing dishes, so that each moment of washing the dishes keeps me aware. If I cannot wash the dishes with a joyful mind, but only want to finish them quickly so I can go drink tea, then I will likewise be unable to enjoy that cup of tea fully and happily. Though the cup of tea is in my hand, my mind is still dwelling on other things; and so the flavor of the tea and the pleasure of drinking it are utterly lost, and my mind is forever suspended in the ‘future,’ never able to live in the ‘present.’”
Remember: what you do does not matter; what matters is being focused and aware in what you do.
Question: Awareness of movements turning without stop is easy to speak of, but very difficult to put into practice. What should I do?

Answer: This is no wonder, for since beginningless kalpas we have formed the habit of endlessly indulging in delusive thinking; habit has become nature, has become instinct, whereas awareness of movements is brand new. To transform a deep-rooted bad habit (delusive thinking) into a brand-new good habit (awareness of movements), one must expend great effort and undergo great training.

There is a story like this: a woman urged her husband to recite the Buddha’s name, but the husband was slack and lazy, idle by nature, and could never manage it. Fearing that he would fall into hell in the future and suffer, the wife said to her husband: “I will hang a little bell on the door. Whenever you go in or out, as soon as you hear the bell, recite the Buddha’s name at once, and you will be kept safe.” The husband replied: “What is so hard about that? I will do as you say.” Thereafter, every time he went in or out and heard the doorbell ring, he would recite the Buddha’s name a few times. He thought this method quite good, saving his wife from constantly prodding him to recite. Time flew like an arrow, the days and months like a shuttle; the husband, now elderly, fell ill and did not rise again, and soon died of his illness. After death he did indeed fall into hell. Because in the world his evil karma had been heavy, he had not believed in wholesome dharmas and had not done good deeds, and so the demon attendants threw him into an iron cauldron to be boiled. It happened that when a demon attendant prodded him with a trident, the copper bell on the trident rang, and the husband, thinking it was the doorbell ringing, recited the Buddha’s name aloud again and again, and so was delivered.

This story tells us that using skillful methods and rules to help form good habits makes it much easier. Now, to form the good habit of awareness of movements, you can lay down rules for yourself: 1. Be aware of the movement when getting up and when sitting down; 2. When walking (including walking indoors), be aware of the movement of every step; 3. When eating, be aware of every mouthful chewed. Before sleeping at night, review how you did today. Grade yourself on five levels — very good (5 points), good (4), fair (3), poor (2), very poor (1) — and record it in a notebook. On the evening of every Sunday, make a summary of the seven days of the week, work out the average score, assess how the week went and how the next week should be improved and raised, and write it all in detail in the notebook. On this basis, make a monthly summary and a yearly summary. This notebook may be named the Record of Self-Knowledge. That people fall rather than rise is because they suffer from being unable to know themselves. Now, with the Record of Self-Knowledge, examining oneself daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly — so long as one carries it out earnestly, there is no fear of failing. The Great Emperor of Mount Tai instructed:
“Doing good,
(blessing)
is like the grass of a spring garden: its growth is unseen, yet it increases day by day; doing evil,
(blessing)
is like a whetstone: its wearing is unseen, yet it diminishes day by day. Calamity and blessing shift in secret
(calamity and blessing shift in the dark)
, and the deluded are unaware
(the deluded cannot perceive it)
For our present study and practice, it may be written as:
Awareness,
(prajñā)
is like the grass of a spring garden: its growth is unseen, yet it increases day by day; delusive thinking,
(prajñā)
is like a whetstone: its wearing is unseen, yet it diminishes day by day. Birth and death shift in secret
(birth and death shift in the dark)
, and the deluded are unaware
(the deluded cannot perceive it)

From now on, whenever you study and practice awareness of sensations, awareness of breathing, awareness of the present moment, awareness of thoughts, or awareness in Buddha-recitation, use the Record of Self-Knowledge, and you are certain to succeed.

Drawing on the worthies of old, here is one more example: Mr. Zhao Kangjing of the Song dynasty used a bottle and black and white beans to work at the mind-ground: when a good thought arose, he dropped in a white bean; when an evil thought arose, he dropped in a black bean. At first the beans in the bottle were more black than white; later white gradually exceeded black. In time, they were purely white with no black. Going further, he reached the state where mind and objects were both forgotten, entering the realm beyond thought; and so even the bottle and the beans were abandoned and no longer used.
Question: To remind myself to be aware at all times and in all places, I am always silently repeating “awareness” — is that all right?
Answer: Yes. This is a very skillful method.

blocks.text: 3. Stages of Progress and Questions Answered

inline.s: In working at awareness of movements, there are generally the following stages of progress:

1. At the beginning, delusive thoughts still arise while one is aware of movements. This is because the power of awareness is weak; so long as one keeps training the supporting exercises, it will improve before long.

2. When one is focused in awareness of movements there are no delusive thoughts, but the slightest slackening and delusive thoughts arise. Considerable effort is needed to return to the state of “awareness of movements means no delusive thoughts.”

3. When aware of movements there are no delusive thoughts; but once one forgets to be aware, one sinks into delusive thinking without knowing it, and only after a while discovers that one has been indulging in delusive thinking. However, as soon as one returns to awareness of movements, the delusive thoughts cease of themselves.

4. When aware of movements there are no delusive thoughts; once one forgets to be aware, one sinks into delusive thinking. But now one can discover fairly quickly that one is indulging in delusive thinking. As soon as one returns to awareness of movements, the delusive thoughts cease of themselves.
5. When aware of movements there are no delusive thoughts; the slightest lapse and delusive thoughts slip in through the gap, but one discovers it in good time.
6. The practice becomes one continuous piece, and delusive thoughts have no gap to enter.

The core of the preliminary practices is to cultivate the power of awareness. Every bit that the power of awareness grows, one is that much more free; so one must seize every opportunity to cultivate it. If difficulties arise in later practice, the problem will always be insufficient power of awareness; once the missing awareness is made up, the problem is solved as it arises.
Question: What is delusive thinking? What is right mindfulness?

Answer: Strictly speaking, whatever is thought is delusive; hence all thoughts and thinkings are delusive thinking, and only no-thought is right mindfulness. But generally speaking, delusive thinking refers to unnecessary and inappropriate thoughts. For example, in Buddha-recitation the name of the Buddha is right mindfulness and other thoughts are delusive thinking; in Chan practice the critical phrase is right mindfulness and other thoughts are delusive thinking; in contemplating the mind, contemplating the present thought is right mindfulness and other thoughts are delusive thinking. In awareness of movements, awareness is right mindfulness and other thoughts are delusive thinking.
Question: If both hands and feet are moving, where should I be aware?

Answer: At the beginning, choose the most convenient point of awareness. For example, when practicing taijiquan the eyes follow the hands, so choose the hand the eyes are fixed on. Once the skill of awareness is ripe, one can be aware of the movement as a whole.
Question: When aware of movements, delusive thoughts still arise. What should I do?

Answer: This is a common phenomenon for beginners. The cause is that the power of awareness is not focused and continuous enough, so that awareness and delusive thinking alternate: one moment aware, the next moment in delusive thinking, and so it feels as though the two run side by side. The remedy is: at the beginning, simply knowing that you are aware is enough. Persevere without letting up, and the power of awareness will of itself become ever more focused and continuous. When the practice matures and awareness is continuous, there is no gap for delusive thoughts to insert themselves. At that point, as soon as one is aware of a movement, delusive thoughts cease of themselves. It is like Westerners coming to China who must use chopsticks to eat. At first they are naturally hopelessly clumsy, but as long as they hold to one rule — to eat, one must use chopsticks — then after long use they naturally go from clumsy to skilled, and from skilled to deft, and from deft to wondrous. So the work of awareness of movements is not difficult; one need only lay down one rule for oneself: when there is movement, one must be aware. Keep it up, and there is no fear that the practice will not be accomplished.
Question: Sometimes I am enveloped by delusive thinking and simply cannot be aware of movements at all. What should I do?

Answer: If that is the case, then stop; do not try to be aware of movements, but calmly watch what the mind is thinking. The key points of this operation are: 1. Watch it; 2. Do not judge the content of what is thought (do not participate). In this way delusive thinking is like a fire burning the sky — after a while it goes out. Then return to awareness of movements. If you are again enveloped by delusive thinking, do the same again. Moreover, the time you spend watching “what the mind is thinking” is not wasted, for you are cultivating the ability to be aware of thoughts. Practice in this way, and both the number of times you are enveloped by delusive thinking and how long it lasts will fall sharply, and the power of awareness will gradually grow strong. In fact, you should often look inward and watch your own thoughts, emotions, and sensations; just watch, without judging. This is very beneficial for reducing delusive thinking and cultivating the power of awareness. Do it often enough, and you will discover its wonder for yourself.
Question: When aware of movements, there is a thought in the mind: awareness. Is that right or not?

Answer: When aware of movements, having the thought “awareness” in the mind is right; this is right mindfulness. All thoughts other than this right mindfulness are delusive thoughts. When you practice to the point where “awareness” is the only thought left, you have accomplished the gathering of ten thousand thoughts into one.
Question: What is eating Chan?

Answer: Eating Chan is making eating itself a Chan practice. The method is: eat slowly, eat with focus, eat with awareness; chew each mouthful at least thirty times, aware of every chew. This not only cultivates the power of awareness, removes delusive thinking, and lets you enjoy tranquility, but is also of great benefit to digestion and absorption.
